s: are_called_to praise of God [clap hands and shout] The nations are commanded to clap their hands and shout to God with triumph. They are also described as being subdued under God's people, and God reigns over them. The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the people of the God of Abraham.

is_a servant of the LORD Abraham is called the LORD's servant, and his offspring are urged to remember the LORD's works. The LORD made a covenant with him, and remembering his holy word and Abraham is why the LORD brought his people out.
Praise of God is a psalm-called act of clapping, shouting and repeated singing to God as King, done with understanding, grounded in his rule over all the earth, nations, and exaltation.

reacts_to_mount_zion_with dismay [saw it, were amazed, hurried away] The kings assembled themselves and passed by together. When they saw the city they were amazed and dismayed, and they hurried away. Trembling took hold of them, with pain like that of a woman in labor.

is_shepherd_of flock [over the foolish appointed to Sheol] Death is described as the shepherd of the foolish, who are appointed as a flock for Sheol. The upright are said to have dominion over them in the morning.

The psalmist is a speaker who summons all peoples to listen, promises wisdom and understanding, plays a riddle on the harp, questions fearing evil days, and affirms God will redeem his soul from Sheol and receive him.

l: peoples (all inhabitants of the world), Psalms
s: The peoples are addressed as the audience of the psalm, low and high, rich and poor together. They are called to hear the psalmist's wisdom.

l: rich who trust in wealth, Psalms
s: A group of rich people who trust in wealth and boast of riches. They cannot ransom a brother or redeem anyone from God, believe their houses last forever, and name lands after themselves, yet they die, leave wealth to others, join their fathers, and, lacking understanding, perish like animals.

cannot_be_carried_in_death nothing carried away [man dies and takes nothing] Wealth cannot buy life or redemption, and it is left to others when its owner dies. A man carries nothing away at death, and his glory does not descend after him.

has_cost costly [no payment is ever enough] The redemption of life is said to be costly, and no payment is ever enough to let someone live forever and not see corruption. No one can give God a ransom for his brother, yet God will redeem the psalmist's soul from Sheol.

fate perish [leave wealth to others] The fool and the senseless perish just as wise men die, and leave their wealth to others. Their destiny, shared by those who approve their sayings, is to be a flock for Sheol with Death as shepherd.

The wicked are a group who hate instruction, forget God, and cast his words aside while claiming his covenant. They side with thieves and adulterers, give their mouths to evil and deceit, and slander their own brother. God, whose silence they mistook for approval, challenges them, will rebuke and accuse them, and warns he will tear them apart.

is_status not rebuked [burnt offerings continually before God] God says he does not rebuke Israel for their sacrifices and that their burnt offerings are continually before him. He states he has no need of a bull from their stall or goats from their pens, since all animals and the world are his, and he would not eat bulls' meat or drink goats' blood. The covenant with his saints was made by sacrifice, but the offerings are not what God ultimately wants.
The sacrifice of thanksgiving is an offering God requires, which he desires in place of animal offerings along with paid vows; whoever offers it glorifies God and prepares the way for his salvation.

l: judgment (God's judgment of his people), Psalms
s: is_called_by God [he calls heavens and earth to judge his people] God calls the heavens above and the earth so that he may judge his people, and the heavens declare his righteousness because God himself is judge. The judgment includes testimony against Israel about sacrifices and a sharper indictment of the wicked for hypocrisy, complicity with thieves and adulterers, deceit, and slander. It ends with a warning of being torn apart for those who forget God and a promise of salvation for those who offer thanksgiving.

Jerusalem is a city of the LORD's house, built compact, where the tribes go up and where thrones of David's house sit for judgment. Surrounded by mountains, it symbolizes the LORD's protection of his people. The records move from devastation, laid in heaps by nations with servants' blood shed around it, through a speaker's prayer for its peace and vow to seek its good, to exile-like longing never to forget it despite Edom's call to raze it. They end with restoration: the LORD builds it up, strengthens its gates, blesses its children, makes peace, and fills it with wheat.

is_present_to David [constantly before him] David says he knows his transgressions and that his sin is constantly before him. He declares that he has sinned against God only and done evil in his sight, that he was born in iniquity and conceived in sin, and he asks to be delivered from the guilt of bloodshed.
Forgiveness and cleansing is what David seeks from God: he pleads for transgressions to be blotted out, washing with hyssop, a clean heart and renewed spirit, ending with restored joy of salvation.

Doeg the Edomite is the man who told Saul that David had come to Ahimelech's house. The psalm addresses him as a boastful 'mighty man' who loves evil, lying and devouring words, wields a deceitful tongue, and trusts in his riches rather than God. It ends by declaring God will destroy him forever, uprooting him from the land of the living.

respond_to_fate_of_doeg fear and laughter [will see it, fear, and laugh at him] The righteous will see God's destruction of the wicked man, fear, and laugh at him. They will say that he did not make God his strength but trusted in his riches and strengthened himself in his wickedness.
The workers of iniquity are a group who devour God's people like bread and never call on God; they are seized by groundless fear, then shamed and rejected by God.
Human corruption is universal: all have turned back and become filthy together, with no one doing good. God, looking down from heaven, finds no one who understands or seeks him.

The enemies are wicked, unchanging, bloodthirsty and deceitful people who do not fear God. They oppress David, prowling the city walls with malice, threats and lies. David asks for their sudden death and descent into Sheol, declaring they will not live out half their days.

David's familiar friend and companion, once a close fellowship partner who walked with him in God's house, proves deceitful. He violates his covenant and raises his hands against friends, his butter-smooth, oil-soft words being drawn swords while his heart harbors war.
A city where David saw violence and strife; enemies prowl its walls day and night, while malice, abuse, destructive forces, threats and lies fill its streets and never leave.

David's many enemies proudly fight him, seeking to swallow him up. They oppress him daily, twist his words, conspire, lurk and watch his steps to take his life; David asks if they escape by iniquity and says they will turn back when he calls on God.

David states that when he is afraid he will put his trust in God, and repeats that he has put his trust in God and will not be afraid. This trust is expressed in the question of what flesh or man can do to him. It rests on his knowledge that God is for him and on God's deliverance of his soul from death.

Enemies of the speaker, likened to lions, with teeth like spears and arrows and tongues like sharp swords, pursue David. They set a net for his steps and dig a pit before him, but fall into it themselves while God rebukes the pursuer.

The wicked are depicted as corrupt from birth: wayward, lying, venomous like a deaf cobra refusing charmers, and plotting injustice and violence in their hearts. The speaker prays for their destruction, asking that their teeth break and they vanish like water, a melting snail, or a stillborn child, ending with the righteous washing his feet in their blood.
The righteous rejoice on seeing vengeance, washing their feet in the wicked's blood; people then affirm that a reward surely awaits the righteous.
Vengeance is what the righteous will see and rejoice over, with the blood of the wicked washing his feet. It is taken as proof that the righteous have a reward and that God judges the earth.

David's enemies are bloodthirsty workers of iniquity who lie in wait for his soul, gather without cause, and curse and lie. They return at evening howling like dogs, prowling the city for food; David asks they be scattered, caught in pride, consumed.

Edom is named in the superscription as the nation of which Joab killed twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt. In God's speech he will throw his sandal on Edom, and the speaker asks who has led him to Edom.
Ephraim is a tribe described as God's helmet and head's defense, yet its bow-armed children turned back in battle and broke God's covenant, so God rejected it and did not choose it.
Judah is the tribe God chose and called his scepter, favored over Joseph's tent and Ephraim, and linked with beloved Mount Zion.

is_rejected_by God [stated in the plea] God's people are described as rejected, broken down, shown hard things, and made to drink wine that makes them stagger. They are also given a banner by God for those who fear him, and are called his beloved. They express confidence that through God they will do valiantly.

l: Plea for restoration and deliverance, Psalms
s: is_a teaching poem [attributed to David] The poem opens by asking God to restore his people and mend the fractures of the quaking land. It continues by asking him to save with his right hand, answer, and give help against the adversary, since human help is vain. It ends with confidence that God will tread down the adversaries.
The king is the subject of a petition that God prolong his life across generations, enthrone him in God's presence forever, and appoint loving kindness and truth to preserve him.

The psalmist, identified as David, is a man under assault, likened to a leaning wall, who declares his soul rests in God alone, urges himself to wait silently, and affirms he will not be greatly shaken.

Assailants are questioned about how long they will assault the psalmist; they intend to topple him from his lofty place, delight in lies, and hypocritically bless with their mouths while cursing inwardly.

l: people (those urged to trust God), Psalms
s: is_urged_to trust in God [at all times] The people are told to trust in God at all times and to pour out their hearts before him, since God is a refuge for them. They are also warned not to trust in oppression, not to become vain in robbery, and not to set their hearts on increasing riches.

comes_from God [psalmist's salvation] Salvation is said to come from God alone, who is the psalmist's rock and salvation. The psalmist's salvation and honor are with God, and this security means he will not be shaken.
The psalmist's refuge is said to be in God, who is also the rock of his strength. God is then declared to be a refuge for the people as well, who are urged to trust him and pour out their hearts.

A group of enemies who seek the psalmist's soul to destroy it. The psalm foretells their doom: they go to the earth's lower parts, fall to the sword, become jackal food, and liars' mouths are silenced.

The psalmist, identified as David, is the author of the psalm. Fearing his enemy, he complains to God and asks to be preserved and hidden from the wicked's conspiracy, affirming God will strike them and the righteous will rejoice.

A noisy crowd of wicked evildoers, enemies of David, conspire together, sharpening tongues like swords and shooting deadly words at innocent men from ambush. They encourage one another in secret snares, asking who will see, but God strikes them down, their own tongues ruin them, and onlookers shake their heads.
The righteous, the upright in heart, are glad in the LORD and take refuge in him, and are finally called to praise him.

l: evil plans and conspiracy (the wicked's plot), Psalms
s: has_aim injustice The wicked's conspiracy involves plotting injustice, laying snares in secret, and declaring they have made a perfect plan. The psalm notes that man's mind and heart are cunning, yet the plot is undone when their own tongues ruin them.

God's judgment is a sudden arrow strike on the wicked, David's enemies, repaying their deadly word-arrows; their own tongues ruin them, onlookers shake their heads, and all mankind fears, declaring and pondering God's work.

God's worshippers are those he chooses and brings near; though sins overwhelmed them, God atoned for transgressions. They are blessed, dwell in his courts, are filled with his house's goodness, are answered by their saving God, and perform vows.
is holy God's house, his holy temple, is the place where the chosen live in his courts. Its goodness is what those he brings near will be filled with.

The earth is visited, watered, and greatly enriched by God, who drenches its furrows, levels its ridges, softens it with showers, and blesses its crop. Its wilderness grasslands overflow, its hills are clothed with gladness, its pastures are covered with flocks, and its valleys are clothed with grain, all shouting and singing for joy. Those who dwell in its faraway places are afraid at God's wonders.

includes showers [soften the earth] God provides grain as he has ordained, using the river of God full of water, drenching furrows and softening the ground with showers to bless the crop. He crowns the year with bounty, and his carts overflow with abundance. The result is overflowing grasslands, flocks on the pastures, and valleys clothed with grain.

All the earth is called to make a joyful shout to God, sing to the glory of his name, and offer praise. It is said that all the earth will worship and sing to God, and the peoples are urged to make the sound of his praise heard.

Israel, the speaker's people, is tested by God like refined silver. They cross the river on foot after the sea becomes dry land, rejoice, endure prison, burdens and oppression, pass through fire and water, and are finally brought to abundance.

A God-fearing speaker who vows to enter God's temple with burnt offerings and pay vows made in distress. He invites all who fear God to hear what God did for his soul, recounts that God heard his cry, notes sin cherished would have blocked it, and ends blessing God.

l: testing and refining of God's people, Psalms
s: God's testing of his people, likened to refining silver, involved imprisonment, burdens, men riding over their heads, and passing through fire and water, ending with God bringing them to abundance.
The psalmist's pledge to enter God's temple with burnt offerings and fulfil vows spoken in distress, specifying fat animals, rams, bulls and goats as the sacrifices.
praise God [called to] The peoples are called on twice, in verses 3 and 5, to praise God, with the refrain "Let all the peoples praise you." They are told that God will judge them with equity.

are_called_to sing for joy [because God judges with equity] The nations are to come to know God's way and salvation. They are urged to be glad and sing for joy because God will judge the peoples with equity and govern the nations on earth.

has_god God [our own God] The community asks God for mercy, blessing, and the shining of his face on them. They hope that through this God's way and salvation will be known among all nations. They state with confidence that the earth has yielded its increase and that God will bless them.

is_received_by us (the psalmist's community) God's blessing is requested in verse 1 and affirmed in verses 6 and 7 as something God will give to the community. The earth's yielded increase is mentioned alongside it. The blessing is linked to a wider purpose: that God's way be known on earth and that all the ends of the earth fear him.
A group who hate God, are asked to scatter like smoke and wax before fire, and face destruction as God strikes their heads; war-loving nations and fleeing armies' kings are scattered.
disposition glad [rejoice before God] The righteous are called to be glad and rejoice with gladness before God. In contrast to the wicked who perish at his presence, they are the ones who rejoice.

l: mountain where God chooses to reign, Psalms
s: is_chosen_by God [for reigning] The rugged mountains of Bashan are asked why they look in envy at this mountain, where God chooses to reign and where the LORD will dwell forever. It is linked to the sanctuary and to the temple at Jerusalem, to which kings will bring presents.

Egypt is a land, also called the land of Ham or tents of Ham, including the field of Zoan, inhabited by a people of foreign language. It is where Jacob lived and Israel increased. God worked signs and wonders there against Pharaoh and his servants, sending plagues of darkness, blood, frogs, flies, lice, hail, locusts, and the death of the firstborn of man and animal. Israel then departed, and Egypt was glad because fear had fallen on it.

A procession of God, the speaker's King, into the sanctuary: singers lead, minstrels follow among tambourine-playing ladies, all calling to bless God, with princes of Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali present.

The psalmist, attributed to David, is God's servant, consumed by zeal for God's house. He suffers hatred without cause, reproach for God's sake, alienation from his brothers, and mockery as the drunkards' song. Weary and dry-throated from crying out, he is given poison and vinegar and finds no comforters. He prays for deliverance, asks judgment on enemies, and vows thankful praise.

The psalmist's enemies are mighty, numerous wrongful foes who hate him without cause, mock him, give him poison and vinegar, and persecute one God has wounded. He responds by asking that their table be a snare, their habitation desolate, and that they be blotted from the book of life.

threatens the psalmist (speaker) [overflowing floods, no foothold] The waters have come up to the psalmist's neck, and he sinks in deep mire with no foothold as the floods overflow him. He prays that the flood waters not overwhelm him, that the deep not swallow him, and that the pit not shut its mouth on him. He asks to be delivered out of the mire and the deep waters.
David's enemies seek his soul, desire his ruin, and mock him with "Aha! Aha!"; David prays they be disappointed, confounded, and turned back in shame.
Worshippers who seek God and love his salvation; David wishes them to rejoice in him and continually declare "Let God be exalted!"

An aged speaker who has taken refuge in the LORD and relied on him since the womb. Fearing abandonment as strength fails, he pleads for rescue, calls himself a marvel to many, and hopes always. After many bitter troubles, he vows to praise with harp and lyre and tell the next generation of God's strength.

The psalmist's enemies conspire against him, watching for his soul and claiming God has forsaken him, urging pursuit since no one will rescue him. He asks that they be disappointed, consumed, and disgraced, and declares them confounded.

fills speaker's mouth [all day long] Praise is the speaker's ongoing commitment: his mouth will be filled with it all day long, and he will add to all of God's praise. He promises to express it by telling of God's righteousness and salvation, and by singing with the harp and lyre, with shouting lips and a redeemed soul. He intends to carry these declarations to the next generation and everyone to come.

The king, a royal son, is the figure for whom justice and righteousness are requested. He judges God's people and the poor rightly, saves the needy, and breaks the oppressor. His dominion spans sea to sea, with tribute and gifts from distant kings and service from all nations. The account closes with his name enduring forever and all nations calling him blessed.

has_helper none [until the king delivers them] The poor and needy are judged with justice by the king, who saves the children of the needy and delivers those who cry out and have no helper. He has pity on them and redeems their souls from oppression and violence, and their blood is precious in his sight.

Justice and righteousness are what the prayer asks God to give the king, and by them he judges God's people and the poor. The hills bring the fruit of righteousness, and in the king's days the righteous flourish with abundant peace.

Asaph, a psalmist who takes refuge in God and is continually with him, nearly slips from envy of the prosperous wicked and doubts his pure living. Silent so as not to betray God's children, he gains understanding in the sanctuary, sees the wicked's end, admits his senselessness, and affirms God upholds him.

The wicked, a proud and violent group, scoff, threaten oppression, deny God's knowledge and are unfaithful to him. They seem always at ease and free of burdens, but in the end they are set in slippery places, destroyed, and perish.

is_dwelling_place_of God [dwelling place of his Name] The sanctuary on Mount Zion, where God has lived, is described as lying in perpetual ruins because of the evil the enemy did in it. Its carved work was broken down, it was burned to the ground, and it was profaned as the dwelling place of God's Name. God is asked to lift up his feet toward its ruins.

is_envied_by the psalmist (Asaph) The wicked's prosperity is what stirred Asaph's envy: they have firm strength, no struggles in death, freedom from the burdens others bear, abundant waters, and ever-increasing riches while always at ease. In the sanctuary Asaph learns that this ease is temporary and is likened to a dream that vanishes on waking.
God destroys the wicked suddenly: Asaph grasps their end in the sanctuary, as God throws them down from slippery places, sweeping them away with terrors, their fantasies dismissed like a dream.

l: God's people (the sheep of God's pasture), Psalms
s: God's people are his flock and inheritance tribe, purchased and redeemed long ago. In their present suffering they see no signs and have no prophet, and none knows its duration. The speaker pleads that God not abandon his dove and poor to beasts, but let the needy praise him.

A hostile group of adversaries who attack God and his people. They roar in the midst of his assembly, set up their standards, hack down the carved work with axes and hammers, burn and profane the sanctuary and all places of worship, resolve in their hearts to crush God's people completely, and reproach and mock his name continually, their tumult rising unceasingly.

The destruction of the sanctuary is an assault by God's adversaries, who roared in the assembly, set up standards, hacked the carved work with axes, hatchet and hammers, then burned the sanctuary and all worship places, profaning God's Name's dwelling. It leaves perpetual ruins, grounding the speaker's plea.
The wicked are arrogant figures warned not to boast or raise their horn of pride and strength; they are made to drink the LORD's foaming cup to its dregs, and their horns are cut off.
has horn (symbol of pride and strength) [will be lifted up] The righteous are mentioned in the closing verse, where it is declared that their horns shall be lifted up, in contrast to the wicked.

The psalmist thanks God and vows to praise the God of Jacob forever. He announces judgment at God's appointed time, warns the arrogant and wicked not to boast, and promises to cut off the wicked's horns and lift up the righteous.

l: cup of wine (the LORD's cup), Psalms
s: contains foaming wine mixed with spices The cup is in the LORD's hand, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. God pours it out, and the wicked of the earth drink it to the very dregs.

l: horn (symbol of pride and strength), Psalms
s: The horn is something the arrogant and wicked are told not to lift up on high. By the end, the horns of the wicked are to be cut off while the horns of the righteous are lifted up.

God's judgment is to be carried out blamelessly at the time he chooses. It brings down one and lifts up another, since exaltation comes from no earthly direction, and it is shown in the cup of wine the wicked must drink to the dregs and in the cutting off of the wicked's horns.
Valiant men lie plundered and dead in Chapter 76; no men of war can lift their hands, showing helplessness before God.

God's judgment on enemies, pronounced from heaven to save the afflicted of the earth. He breaks weapons, puts chariot and horse into a dead sleep, and cuts off princes' spirits. The earth fears and falls silent; survivors of his wrath are restrained.

Asaph, a psalm author, is overwhelmed in a day of trouble, crying to God day and night and refusing comfort. He asks searching questions about God's favor, then resolves to remember and meditate on the LORD's ancient deeds and wonders.
Joseph, sent by the LORD before his people, was sold as a slave and shackled, but after his word proved true the king freed him and made him lord of his house.

Moses is a man of God and servant of the LORD, chosen by him. He is credited with a prayer in which he speaks for the people, confessing their frailty and sin and asking for wisdom, compassion and established work. He is named among the LORD's priests who called on him, were answered, and kept his testimonies and statute. He was sent with Aaron to perform wonders among the Egyptians. Envied in the camp, he stood in the breach to turn away God's wrath, though at Meribah the people's rebellion troubled him and he spoke rashly.
Aaron, a chosen saint and priest of the LORD named with Moses, called on him and was answered, kept his testimonies and statute, and was forgiven though vengeance fell on his doings.

l: people of God (sons of Jacob and Joseph), Psalms
s: The sons of Jacob and Joseph are God's people, the sheep of his pasture. They were redeemed by his arm and led like a flock by Moses and Aaron, yet the psalmist asks whether the Lord will reject them forever. Later they suffer killing, unburied dead, imprisonment, and scorn from neighbors. They plead for mercy and forgiveness, promising thanks and praise to all generations.
The sea, the great waters, writhes and convulses at seeing God, who passes through it by paths whose footsteps remain unknown.

l: storm (thunder, lightning and rain at the sea), Psalms
s: includes thunder, lightning and rain [accompanied God's appearing] The clouds poured out water and the skies resounded with thunder. God's arrows flashed around, the voice of his thunder was in the whirlwind, and the lightnings lit up the world so that the earth trembled and shook.

l: redemption of God's people (the Exodus), Psalms
s: God's redemption of his people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph, by his arm; he led them like a flock through the sea by an unseen path, under Moses and Aaron.

l: God's past deeds and wonders, Psalms
s: attributed_to God [remembered by the psalmist] The psalmist turns to the days of old and the years of the right hand of the Most High as grounds for appeal. He vows to remember and meditate on the LORD's deeds, wonders and work, noting that God made his strength known among the peoples and displayed power over the waters and in the storm.

l: psalmist's distress and doubt about God's rejection, Psalms
s: The psalmist's anguished doubt in Chapter 77: sleepless, comfortless and speechless, he asks whether God rejects forever, whether loving kindness and promise have failed, or compassion been forgotten in anger, then answers by remembering God's past deeds.

l: Israelites (the fathers and their offspring), Psalms
s: The Israelites, the fathers and their descendants, are a people given God's covenant and commands to pass to their children, yet remembered as a stubborn, rebellious generation with disloyal hearts. Despite wonders in Egypt, they forgot God, rebelled at the Red Sea, made a calf, joined Baal Peor and sacrificed children to idols. Oppressed by enemies, they cry out; God remembers his covenant, and the psalmist prays for rescue.

The Red Sea is a place where God performed an awesome work: rebuked, it dried up and was divided, letting rebellious Israel pass through its middle as through a desert, while its waters covered and overthrew Pharaoh's army, leaving none of their adversaries.

is_location_of God's provision and Israel's rebellion In the wilderness God leads Israel like a flock, splits rocks, and brings streams out of the rock for them to drink. It is also where they repeatedly rebel, grieve him, and demand food, doubting that God can prepare a table there.

is_a bread of angels [food from the sky] God rained manna down from the sky for Israel to eat, called the bread of angels, sent in fullness. It was given even as the people doubted he could provide bread.

is_a winged birds [rained as meat on Israel] God sent meat like dust and winged birds like the sand of the seas, driven by the east and south winds and falling in the middle of Israel's camp. The people ate and were filled, but while the food was still in their mouths his anger struck down some of their strongest and the young men.

includes flies, frogs, locusts, hail [sent by God] God's signs in Egypt included turning rivers to blood, swarms of flies, frogs, caterpillars and locusts, hail on vines, sycamore figs, and livestock, and a band of evil angels. Pestilence and the striking of all the firstborn followed. Israel is rebuked for forgetting these deeds.

has_part tent [God abandoned it] Shiloh's tent was where God had placed his dwelling among men. After Israel's idolatry and high places, God abandoned it and delivered his strength and glory into the adversary's hand.

The nations are an enemy group who invade God's inheritance, defile his temple, ruin Jerusalem, leave servants' bodies unburied, devour Jacob, and ignorantly mock God. The record ends with the speaker pleading for wrath and vengeance on them.

God's people, named Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, suffer: fed bread of tears, contended over by neighbors, mocked by enemies. They cry for rescue and promise loyalty and prayer to God's name if revived.

The vine is Israel, brought out of Egypt and planted by the LORD God of Armies after the nations were driven out. It took deep root, filled the land, covered mountains, and stretched branches to the sea and shoots to the River. Then its walls were broken down, so passersby pluck it, the boar and wild animals ravage it, and it is burned and cut down.

l: man of God's right hand, Psalms
s: He is called the son of man whom God made strong for himself. The psalmist asks that God's hand be upon him, and links this to the people's promise not to turn away and to call on God's name once revived.

A plea for restoration addressed to the Chief Musician, set to the tune "The Lilies of the Covenant." Its refrain, "Turn us again... cause your face to shine, and we will be saved," recurs in verses 3, 7, and 19, the divine title growing fuller each time, alongside requests to save, look down, visit the vine, and revive.

l: festival worship (New Moon, full moon, feast day), Psalms
s: The psalm calls for music with tambourine, lyre, harp and trumpet at the New Moon, the full moon and on the feast day. It states this is a statute for Israel and an ordinance of the God of Jacob, appointed in Joseph as a covenant.

The Exodus from Egypt is the LORD's bringing Israel out of bondage, recalled across several chapters. God removed the burden from their shoulders and freed their hands from the basket, and he cites this deliverance as the basis for forbidding foreign gods. It began with striking the Egyptian firstborn and bringing Israel out with a strong hand and outstretched arm. The people left with silver and gold, with no feeble person among the tribes, while Egypt was glad at their departure. The sea was divided, Israel passed through, and Pharaoh's army was overthrown. The LORD then led them through the wilderness with a cloud, fire at night, quails, bread of the sky and water from the rock, bringing them out with joy and singing. Judah became his sanctuary and Israel his dominion, and the sea, Jordan and mountains reacted.
The great assembly is the setting in which God presides and judges among the gods. It is where the charge of unjust judgment and the commands to defend the weak are delivered.

The gods are judged rulers called sons of the Most High. They are accused of unjust judgment and partiality to the wicked, and commanded to defend the weak, poor, fatherless and needy. Ignorant and walking in darkness as earth's foundations shake, they are sentenced to die like men.

oppresses the weak and poor (the oppressed) [victims to be delivered from their hand] The wicked are the ones to whom the gods show partiality in judgment. The needy are to be delivered out of the hand of the wicked.

l: the weak and poor (the oppressed), Psalms
s: is_owed defense and rights [gods are commanded to defend them] The weak, the poor, the fatherless, and the oppressed are those whom the gods are commanded to defend, whose rights are to be maintained, and who are to be rescued and delivered from the hand of the wicked. Their need implies they have not been receiving just treatment.

Unjust judgment is the charge God brings against the gods, expressed as judging unjustly and showing partiality to the wicked. It is linked in the text to the gods' darkness and lack of understanding and to the shaking of the earth's foundations.

A coalition of God's haters, united as one mind, conspires against Israel to destroy it as a nation. It comprises Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre and Assyria; the speaker finally prays they be confounded, made like chaff, and perish.

l: plea for God's judgment on enemies, Psalms
s: is_a psalm [song] The psalmist asks God to act against the coalition, citing the fate of Midian, Sisera, Jabin at Kishon, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna. The requests include making them like chaff, pursuing them with tempest and storm, and filling their faces with confusion. The stated purpose is that they may seek God's name and know that He alone is the Most High over all the earth.

The LORD of Armies, also called LORD God, God of Jacob and King, is addressed by the psalmist in Chapter 84. His dwellings are lovely and the psalmist asks him to hear prayer. He is a sun and shield who gives grace and glory, withholds no good from the blameless, and blesses those who trust him.

l: dwellings of the LORD (courts and house), Psalms
s: The LORD's dwellings, courts, and house are lovely, the object of the psalmist's fainting longing. Sparrows and swallows nest near his altars, dwellers there are blessed and praising, and a single day in his courts surpasses a thousand elsewhere.

The psalmist is a worshipper who longs and faints for the LORD's courts, calling the LORD of Armies his King and God. He prays to be heard, prefers being a doorkeeper in God's house over dwelling in wickedness's tents, and ends by blessing the one who trusts the LORD.

l: pilgrims (those whose strength is in God), Psalms
s: Pilgrims, blessed because their strength is in God and their hearts are set on pilgrimage, turn the valley of Weeping into springs with autumn rain's blessings, grow from strength to strength, and each appears before God in Zion.

will_yield increase The land is described as having received the LORD's favor. It is the place where glory is to dwell, where truth springs out of the earth, and where the land will yield its increase when the LORD gives what is good.

The people have been forgiven their iniquity and had all their sin covered, yet they plead to be turned, relieved of God's indignation, and revived so they may rejoice in him. God will speak peace to them, his saints, but they are warned not to turn again to folly.

The LORD's wrath is directed at humanity, under which all their days pass. In one psalm it is said to be fully taken away, yet the psalmist asks whether it will last forever. In the later psalm it consumes and troubles people, and the speaker pleads that the Lord relent.

is_near people of God [those who fear him] God is addressed as the God of our salvation, and the psalmist asks the LORD to grant it. It is declared to be near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in the land.
meets_together_with Truth Mercy is pictured as meeting together with truth. It is part of the vision of reconciliation in verse 10.
springs_out_of earth Truth meets together with mercy and is said to spring out of the earth. It is part of the psalm's picture of restoration in the land.
Righteousness is personified: it kisses peace, looks down from heaven, and goes before the LORD, preparing the way for his steps.
God will speak peace to his people, his saints. Peace is pictured as kissing righteousness.

l: the proud and violent men (David's enemies), Psalms
s: A group of proud, violent men who hate David and disregard God, rising against him and seeking his life; David asks for a sign of the Lord's goodness to shame them.

David's prayer is spoken aloud with his voice and takes the form of a complaint and a plea for mercy. It moves from describing his troubles and abandonment to declaring the LORD his refuge, then asks for a hearing, deliverance from persecutors, and release from prison so he may give thanks. It ends with the expectation that the righteous will surround him because the LORD will be good to him.
is_among those who acknowledge the LORD [recorded by the LORD] Babylon is the foreign land where the exiles sit weeping by its rivers. The willows there hold the harps the exiles have hung up.

The peoples are to be counted and written up by the LORD, who says of each "This one was born there." Named among them are Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia, who are recorded as among those who acknowledge him.

l: the dead (those in the grave), Psalms
s: has_state cut off from God's hand The dead are described as the slain who lie in the grave, remembered by God no more and cut off from his hand. Heman compares himself to them and asks whether they rise to praise the LORD or whether his wonders, loving kindness, faithfulness, and righteousness are known in the grave, Destruction, the dark, and the land of forgetfulness.
Heman's friends, in Chapter 88, are those the LORD has taken from him and made regard him as an abomination; by the end they are placed far from him, in darkness.
God's wrath and terrors weigh heavily on Heman in Chapter 88: fierce wrath passes over him, LORD's waves afflict him, and terrors cut him off and distract him, engulfing him like water all day.

is_directed_to LORD [comes before him in the morning] Heman's prayer is a daily cry, day and night, with hands spread out to the LORD. He asks that it enter the LORD's presence and says it comes before him in the morning, though the psalm records no answer.

David's offspring are promised by the LORD to endure forever, with a throne lasting like heaven, sun, and moon. If they forsake the law, they face the rod and stripes, yet the LORD keeps his loving kindness and faithfulness.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant with David), Psalms
s: The LORD's covenant with David is a sworn promise, firm forever, to establish David's offspring and throne; the LORD will not break or alter it. Chapter 89 states it, then the psalmist laments an apparent renunciation. Chapter 132 reaffirms the oath, extending it to later generations on condition that David's children keep the covenant and testimony.

will_be beaten down [promised by the LORD] The LORD promises that no enemy will tax David and no wicked man will oppress him, and that he will beat down his adversaries and strike those who hate him. In the lament, the situation is reversed: the LORD has exalted the right hand of David's adversaries, made his enemies rejoice, and passers-by rob the anointed, while enemies mock the footsteps of the LORD's anointed one.

The psalmist charges that the LORD, angry with his anointed, has rejected him: renouncing the covenant, defiling his crown, breaking his defenses, turning back his sword, ending his splendor, throwing down his throne, and shaming him. It closes with a plea asking how long the LORD will hide and where his former kindness is.

Humanity is portrayed as frail and short-lived, living seventy to eighty years of labor and sorrow, compared to grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening. Consumed and troubled by God's anger, with sins exposed, people end like a sigh and ask to be taught to count their days.

Human mortality, caused by the Lord turning man to destruction, is brief: seventy to eighty years of labor and sorrow, fleeting against God's thousand years, leading the prayer to urge counting days for a wise heart.
The psalmist says that if the LORD kept a record of sins, no one could stand. The chapter ends with the promise that the LORD will redeem Israel from all their sins.

The faithful one makes the LORD their refuge and dwelling place, loving him and knowing his name. Protected from pestilence, terror by night, arrows by day, and destruction at noon, they remain unafraid. Angels bear them up, they trample lion, cobra, and serpent, and they only witness the recompense of the wicked. The LORD promises to deliver, honor, and satisfy them with long life.

is_provided_by LORD [shadow of the Almighty, under his wings] Refuge and protection form the chapter's central theme: the LORD is a refuge and fortress, his wings give shelter, and his faithfulness is a shield and rampart. Protection covers threats by night and day, including the fowler's snare, pestilence, and destruction, and extends through angels who guard the faithful in all their ways and keep them from dashing a foot against a stone. Those who make the LORD their refuge are promised that evil and plague will not come near their dwelling.

The psalmist is a person gladdened by the LORD's work. He is exalted like a wild ox with fresh anointing, and though wicked enemies rise against him, he has seen and heard of them while he triumphs in the LORD's works.

l: the wicked (enemies of the LORD), Psalms
s: The wicked, enemies of the LORD, spring up like grass and flourish for a time, but they will perish, be destroyed forever and scattered; only fools miss this.

The righteous are portrayed as flourishing like palm trees and growing like Lebanon cedars. Planted in the LORD's house and courts, they thrive there and, even in old age, keep bearing fruit, full of sap and green, showing the LORD is upright.

is_a good thing Giving thanks and singing praises to the LORD is called a good thing, to be done by proclaiming his loving kindness in the morning and his faithfulness every night. It is accompanied by the ten-stringed lute, the harp, and the melody of the lyre.

l: floods (the floods and waters of the sea), Psalms
s: The floods lift up their voice and their waves, repeated three times in the address to the LORD. The many waters and mighty breakers of the sea make great noise, but the LORD on high is said to be mightier than them.

The wicked are arrogant boasters who afflict the LORD's people, killing the widow, alien and fatherless. They believe the LORD will not see, hold a throne of wickedness that makes mischief by statute, and condemn innocent blood. Ultimately a pit is dug for them, and the LORD brings their own iniquity upon them and cuts them off.

The psalmist is a speaker who depends on the LORD as help and comfort. He cries for vengeance against the wicked, recalls being upheld when his foot slipped, and ends delighting in the LORD's comforts, calling Him high tower and rock of refuge.

follow judgment [will follow it] Those who love the LORD are told to hate evil, and the LORD preserves their souls and delivers them from the hand of the wicked. Light is sown for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart, and they are urged to be glad in the LORD and give thanks to his holy Name.

Vengeance belongs to the LORD; the psalmist calls God to rise as judge and repay the proud. Judgment will return to righteousness, the upright follow it, and the LORD brings the wicked's iniquity upon them, cutting them off.

The speakers call one another to sing to the LORD, shout aloud, come before him with thanksgiving, worship, bow down, and kneel. They identify themselves as his people and sheep and are urged to hear his voice today and not harden their hearts as at Meribah and Massah.

The fathers tempted and tested the LORD at Meribah and Massah in the wilderness, though they saw his work. He was grieved with that generation for forty years, calling them a people who err in their heart and have not known his ways. He swore in wrath that they would not enter his rest.

is_directed_to the LORD [singing, thanksgiving, bowing] Worship and praise are the opening and central call of the chapter: singing, shouting aloud, thanksgiving, songs, bowing down, and kneeling before the LORD. They are grounded in his greatness as King and Maker and in his care for his people. The chapter ties them to hearing his voice and not hardening the heart.
The whole earth is commanded to sing to the LORD, tremble before him, and rejoice; it is established and immovable, and is the object of the LORD's coming judgment.

The nations are to hear the LORD's glory, marvelous works, and salvation declared among them, and the families of nations are told to ascribe glory and strength to him. They are also told that the LORD reigns and that he will judge the peoples with equity.
is_a idols The gods of the peoples are declared to be idols, in contrast to the LORD who made the heavens. The LORD is said to be feared above all gods.

The LORD's right hand and holy arm have worked salvation for him. He has made it known and openly shown his righteousness in the sight of the nations. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God.

The LORD is said to be coming to judge the earth, and the coming is stated twice for emphasis. He will judge the peoples with equity, and the world with righteousness and with his truth, and creation is called to rejoice before him because of it.

is_commanded_to rejoice The earth is called to rejoice, and it sees the LORD's lightning and trembles. The mountains melt like wax at his presence, and he is declared Lord of the whole earth and most high above it.

l: idol worshippers (those who serve engraved images), Psalms
s: Those who serve engraved images and boast in their idols are to be shamed. The gods they serve are commanded to worship the LORD, who is exalted far above them.

The idols are objects of silver and gold made by men's hands; they have mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet but cannot speak, see, hear, smell, feel or walk, and their makers and trusters become like them.

l: all the earth (the inhabitants of the earth), Psalms
s: All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God. The earth is told to make a joyful noise, burst out and sing for joy, and sing praises with harp, voice, trumpets, and ram's horn. The sea, the world and those who dwell in it, the rivers, and the mountains are also called to roar, clap, and sing before the LORD.

l: new song (song to the LORD), Psalms
s: The psalm opens by commanding that a new song be sung to the LORD because he has done marvelous things. Praise is to be given with joyful noise, the harp and the voice of melody, trumpets, and the ram's horn before the King.
The LORD is said to be coming to judge the earth, and this is the reason creation is to sing before him. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.
Samuel is one who calls on the LORD's name; the LORD answered him, spoke to him among others, and he kept the LORD's testimonies and statute.

is_commanded_to shout for joy to the LORD [call to worship] All the lands are addressed directly and commanded to shout for joy to the LORD. Together with the other worshippers, they are urged to serve him with gladness and to come before his presence with singing.

is_offered_to the LORD [on entering his gates and courts] Thanksgiving and praise are the prescribed manner of approaching the LORD, with worshippers entering his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise. They are also to give thanks to him and bless his name, because he is good and his loving kindness and faithfulness endure.

David, speaking as a ruler, commits to praising the LORD and singing of loving kindness and justice. He resolves to live blamelessly in his house, rejecting evil, faithless deeds, slander, arrogance and deceit. He favors the faithful, wanting them near him, and ends by vowing to destroy the wicked of the land every morning.

l: the wicked of the land, Psalms
s: is_a worker of iniquity [to be cut off from the city] The wicked of the land, also described as workers of iniquity, are the target of the speaker's resolve. He says he will destroy them morning by morning and cut them off from the LORD's city.
Loving kindness and justice are the subjects of the speaker's song, which he sings as praise to the LORD.
A blameless life is something the speaker resolves to live carefully, with a blameless heart within his house. He also says that those who walk in a perfect way will serve him.

An afflicted psalmist cries out in distress, likened to a lonely pelican and a sparrow on a housetop. Enemies reproach him all day, and the LORD has weakened and cast him aside in indignation. He ends by pleading not to be taken in mid-life, affirming that God's servants' children will endure.

is_directed_to LORD [poured out in prayer] The distress is expressed in images of smoke, burning bones, withered grass, groaning, loneliness as a pelican, owl, and sparrow, eating ashes like bread, and mixing drink with tears. It is attributed to the LORD's indignation and wrath, and the speaker brings it before him as a prayer for a quick answer, noting that his strength and days have been cut short.

l: God's eternity versus human transience, Psalms
s: contrasts heavens and earth perish while God endures [they wear out like a garment] The speaker's days are likened to a long shadow and withering grass, while the LORD remains forever and his renown endures to all generations. The earth's foundations and the heavens, God's own works, will perish and wear out like a garment, but God is the same and his years have no end, and the servants' children will be established before him.

is_exhorted_to praise the LORD [all within David praises his holy name] David's soul is addressed repeatedly and told to praise the LORD's holy name with all that is within him. It is urged not to forget the LORD's benefits, and the psalm closes by again telling it to praise the LORD.

receive righteousness to children's children [those who keep his covenant] Those who fear the LORD receive loving kindness as great as the heavens are high above the earth. The LORD has compassion on them as a father has on his children, and his loving kindness is from everlasting to everlasting with them, with his righteousness extending to their children's children.

The LORD's works are wondrous, mighty and awesome, found in all places of his dominion; generations commend them, his tender mercies cover them, he is gracious in them, and all his works give thanks to him.

l: LORD's loving kindness and mercy, Psalms
s: The LORD's loving kindness and mercy are abundant, crowning the speaker; directed toward those who fear him, it is as vast as the heavens above earth and endures from everlasting to everlasting.

removes_transgressions_distance as far as east from west The LORD is said to forgive all sins and not to deal with us according to our sins or repay us for our iniquities. He has removed our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west.

l: throne and kingdom of the LORD, Psalms
s: The LORD's throne and kingdom in the heavens rules over all; glorious, majestic and everlasting, its dominion endures through all generations, and the saints speak of its glory.

The psalmist, speaking in Chapter 104, calls his soul to bless the LORD, his God. He vows lifelong song, hopes his meditation pleases, promises to rejoice in the LORD, and ends by asking that sinners and the wicked be removed.

is_filled_with fruit of the LORD's works The earth was founded by the LORD so that it should not be moved forever, and was once covered by the deep with waters standing above the mountains. At the LORD's rebuke the waters fled, the mountains rose and the valleys sank, and a boundary now keeps the waters from covering it again. It is watered, filled with the fruit of the LORD's works and riches, and trembles when he looks at it.

depend_on LORD [for food] Wild donkeys, birds, livestock, wild goats, rock badgers, storks, and forest animals are shown drinking from the springs, nesting in trees, and finding refuge in the high mountains and rocks. Young lions roar after prey and seek their food from God, then lie down in their dens at sunrise. In the sea, innumerable small and large creatures and leviathan live, and all wait on the LORD for food, are satisfied when he opens his hand, and die when he takes away their breath.

The psalm presents creation as the LORD's wise work and ongoing provision: springs and rain, grass for livestock, plants, wine, oil, and bread for man, and trees for birds. The moon and sun mark seasons and the cycle of night and day, in which animals prowl and man labors. All creatures depend on him for food in due season, and he renews the face of the ground by sending out his Spirit.

l: Egyptian enemies (adversaries at the Red Sea), Psalms
s: have_heart_turned_to hate God's people [turned by the LORD] The Egyptians had their hearts turned by the LORD to hate his people and conspire against his servants. They did not rebel against his words of darkness, and they suffered the plagues. They were glad when Israel left, since fear of them had fallen on them.
Canaan is the land promised to Israel as inheritance, pledged when the patriarchs were few foreigners there; it holds idols to which children were sacrificed.

l: covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Psalms
s: An everlasting covenant the LORD remembers forever, made with Abraham, sworn as an oath to Isaac, and confirmed to Jacob and Israel as a statute, promising the land of Canaan as their inheritance.
A series of divine plagues on Egypt sent by the LORD: blood-turned waters, frogs, flies, lice, hail, locusts and darkness, destroying crops and fish, culminating in the death of all firstborn.
The fathers made a calf in Horeb and worshiped it as a molten image. By doing so they exchanged their glory for the image of a bull that eats grass, forgetting God their Savior.

l: Israel's repeated rebellion and God's mercy, Psalms
s: is_a pattern of rebellion followed by rescue The psalm sets out a pattern in which the people believe and sing praise, then soon forget God's works and rebel, as at the Red Sea, in the desert, at Horeb, at Baal Peor, at Meribah and in Canaan. Each time God judges them but also saves, finally regarding their distress and remembering his covenant according to his loving kindnesses. The psalm says he rescued them many times, though they were rebellious in their counsel.

l: the redeemed (redeemed by the LORD), Psalms
s: The redeemed are called to give thanks and say so, having been redeemed from the hand of the adversary. They are described as gathered out of the lands from east, west, north, and south.

l: wanderers in the wilderness (gathered from the lands), Psalms
s: They wandered in a desert way, found no city to live in, and were hungry and thirsty until their soul fainted. They cried to the LORD, who delivered them and led them by a straight way to a city to live in. They are told to praise him because he satisfies the longing soul and fills the hungry with good.

l: prisoners in darkness (those who rebelled against God), Psalms
s: They sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in affliction and iron, because they rebelled against God's words and condemned the counsel of the Most High. Their hearts were brought down with labor and no one helped, but when they cried to the LORD he saved them, brought them out, and broke their chains. He broke the gates of bronze and cut the bars of iron for them.

Fools are afflicted because of their disobedience and iniquities, so that their soul abhors all food and they draw near the gates of death. When they cry to the LORD, he saves them, sending his word to heal them and deliver them from their graves. They are urged to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare his deeds with singing.

l: seafarers (those who go down to the sea in ships), Psalms
s: Seafarers who do business in great waters see the LORD's deeds and wonders in the deep. When he raises a stormy wind they mount to the sky and sink to the depths, reel like drunken men, and reach their wits' end. They cry to him, he stills the storm, and he brings them to their desired haven, and they are urged to exalt him in the assembly and among the elders.

endures forever The LORD's loving kindness is said to endure forever and is the reason given for thanks and praise after each deliverance. The chapter ends by telling the wise to pay attention and consider the LORD's loving kindnesses.

l: desert and fruitful land (transformed land), Psalms
s: The LORD turns rivers into desert, water springs into thirsty ground, and fruitful land into a salt waste because of the wickedness of those who dwell there. He also turns desert into a pool of water and dry land into springs, where the hungry live, prepare a city, sow fields, plant vineyards, and reap increase.

David, the speaker, is a worshipper with a steadfast heart toward God. He resolves to sing, wake the dawn with harp and lyre, and thank the LORD among nations. He then turns to lament God's rejection of the people, asks who will lead him to the fortified city, pleads for help, and ends confident of valor through God.
is_beloved_of God The beloved are those the speaker asks God to deliver by saving with his right hand and answering. The request is made so that they may be delivered.
The enemies are the adversary against whom the speaker asks God for help, since the help of man is vain. The speaker expresses confidence that God will tread them down.
God's loving kindness, described as great above the heavens, and faithfulness, reaching to the skies, are the stated reasons for the speaker's thanks and praise among nations.

The speaker resolves to give thanks to the LORD among the nations and to sing praises to him among the peoples. This is accompanied by singing, music with the soul, and the waking of harp and lyre and of the dawn.

David's adversaries open wicked and deceitful mouths against him, surround him with words of hatred, fight him without cause, and repay his love with hostility and evil for good. They shake their heads at him in scorn. David asks that they be clothed with dishonor and covered with their own shame as with a robe, and says they will be shamed when they arise.

The wicked man is the target of David's detailed curses: an adversary set over him, a guilty verdict, a prayer turned to sin, few days, loss of his office, a widowed wife, beggar children, plundered possessions, and a name blotted out. The reasons given are that he showed no kindness, persecuted the poor, needy, and broken-hearted to kill them, and loved cursing, which clothed him like a garment and soaked into him like water and oil.

In this unit the psalm opens with a complaint about lying enemies, moves into an extended series of curses on a wicked man and his family in verses 6-19, and declares in verse 20 that this is the LORD's reward to David's adversaries. It then turns to David's own plea and ends with a vow of thanks and praise.

David asks the LORD to deliver him for his name's sake and because his loving kindness is good, citing his poverty, wounded heart, fading strength, and weakness from fasting. He says he wants the rescue to show that it is the LORD's hand, and he is confident that the LORD will stand at the right hand of the needy to save him. He promises great thanks and public praise in return.

David's Lord is a royal figure commanded to sit at the LORD's right hand and rule among his enemies. His people willingly serve him on the day of his power, and he is sworn a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. He crushes kings in wrath, judges nations, and crushes the ruler of the whole earth. He drinks from the brook on the way and lifts up his head.

The enemies are to be made a footstool for the feet of David's Lord, who is to rule among them. Kings and the ruler of the whole earth are to be crushed in the day of his wrath, and dead bodies will be heaped up among the nations.

l: those who trust in the LORD (the LORD's people), Psalms
s: The LORD's people are those who trust him: shown his works' power, given the nations' heritage, granted redemption and an eternal covenant, then likened to immovable Mount Zion, surrounded by the LORD forever.

The LORD's works are great, honorable and majestic, pondered by those who delight in them; they embody truth and justice, with precepts sure, established forever and done uprightly, and he has made them remembered.
Wisdom is said to have its beginning in the fear of the LORD. Those who do his work are said to have a good understanding.
is beginning of wisdom The fear of the LORD is declared the beginning of wisdom. Those who fear him are the ones to whom the LORD gives food.

l: the man who fears the LORD, Psalms
s: The man who fears the LORD is blessed, delighting greatly in the commandments and being gracious, merciful, and righteous. He lends and gives to the poor, and has mighty offspring and wealth. Trusting the LORD with a steadfast heart, he is never shaken and fears no evil news. He ends unafraid of adversaries, remembered forever, his horn exalted with honor.
The wicked are a group who witness the blessing and honor of the God-fearing man, grieve and gnash their teeth, then melt away as their desire perishes.

The servants of the LORD are a group called to serve and praise him. In one psalm they are urged to praise his name now and forever; in another they stand by night in his house, lifting their hands in the sanctuary in praise.
The LORD raises the poor out of the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He sets him with princes, even the princes of his people.
becomes joyful mother of children [settled in her home] The LORD settles the barren woman in her home. She becomes a joyful mother of children.
is_a sanctuary [of God, when Israel went out of Egypt] Judah became God's sanctuary when Israel went out of Egypt.
flees_at Exodus from Egypt [saw it and fled] The sea saw it and fled. It is then asked why it fled.
compared_to rams [skipped like] The mountains skipped like rams. They are asked what caused them to do so.
compared_to lambs [skipped like] The little hills skipped like lambs. They are asked why they did so.
The house of Aaron is exhorted to trust in the LORD, who is their help and shield. The LORD will bless the house of Aaron.

l: those who fear the LORD, Psalms
s: Those who fear the LORD are a group of his servants who stand in his house and courts. They are urged to trust him as help and shield, promised blessing for small and great and their children, then called to praise him, with his compassion.

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by human hands. Though they have mouths, eyes, and ears, they cannot speak, see, or hear, and have no breath. Those who make and trust them will become like them.

The psalmist is a devoted servant of the LORD, son of his servant girl, who loves the LORD because he was heard. Surrounded by the cords of death and Sheol, he called on the LORD's name and was saved and freed from chains. He resolves to call on the LORD all his life, walk before him, take the cup of salvation, offer thanksgiving, and pay his vows publicly in Jerusalem.
All the nations, along with all peoples, are called on to praise the LORD and extol him. No response is recorded in this unit; it is only a summons.

l: loving kindness (the LORD's loving kindness), Psalms
s: The LORD's loving kindness is said to be great toward 'us'. It is given as a reason for the nations and peoples to praise him.
The LORD's faithfulness is said to endure forever. It is given, together with his loving kindness, as grounds for praising him.

The psalmist is a speaker who calls the LORD his God. Distressed and surrounded by nations, he cried out, was answered with freedom and helped, though disciplined but not given over to death. He takes refuge in the LORD, fears no man, and vows to live, give thanks, and exalt God.

are_compared_to bees [surrounding the speaker] The nations surrounded the speaker on all sides, like bees. In the LORD's name the speaker cut them off, and they are said to be quenched like burning thorns.

The psalmist is a servant of the LORD, who holds the LORD as his portion yet sees himself as a stranger on the earth, small and despised. He vows to keep, meditate on, and love the LORD's law, and prays for teaching and revival. Afflicted and persecuted by the proud and wicked, he does not forget the law, rises at midnight, and praises seven times daily. He hates falsehood, befriends those who fear the LORD, and ends confessing he has strayed like a lost sheep, asking to be sought.

l: the proud and wicked (enemies of the psalmist), Psalms
s: The proud and wicked are the psalmist's enemies: callous-hearted, far from and forsaking the LORD's law, lacking his salvation. They slander, mock, persecute, and trap the psalmist with pits, snares, and lies. The LORD rebukes them, rejects the straying, and discards them like dross; the psalmist grieves and asks that they be disappointed.

The psalmist is a speaker in distress who cried to the LORD and was answered. He asks deliverance from lying lips and deceitful tongues, laments living in Meshech among Kedar's tents with one who hates peace, and declares himself for peace while others choose war.

l: lying lips and deceitful tongue (the speaker's slanderers), Psalms
s: is_for war [when the speaker speaks] The lying lips and deceitful tongue are what the speaker asks the LORD to deliver his soul from. The deceitful tongue is addressed directly and asked what will be given and done to it, with the answer being sharp arrows of the mighty and coals of juniper.

l: him who hates peace (the speaker's neighbor), Psalms
s: hates peace He is the one with whom the speaker's soul has dwelt too long. He hates peace, and the speaker notes that when he speaks for peace, they are for war.

A Psalm speaker, first among exiles ('we', then 'I'), who looks to the hills for help, vows loyalty to Jerusalem under a self-curse, prizes it above chief joy, calls the LORD to remember Edom, and blesses Babylon's avenger.
The LORD's keeping is protection that steadies the foot, shields from sun, moon and all evil, guards the soul, and covers every going out and coming in forevermore.
The LORD's tribes belong to the LORD and go up to Jerusalem according to an ordinance for Israel, ultimately to give thanks to the LORD's name.

The psalmist, in a psalm attributed to David, rejoices at being invited to the LORD's house and now stands in Jerusalem's gates. He urges prayer for its peace, blesses it for his brothers and companions, and resolves to seek its good for the LORD's house.

Peace is what the speaker urges others to pray for on Jerusalem's behalf, with the promise that those who love the city will prosper. He wishes it within Jerusalem's walls and says to the city, "Peace be within you."

A group who call the LORD 'our God' look to him like servants watching a master's hand. Having endured much contempt and scoffing from the proud and those at ease, they plead for his mercy, ending in a petition.

l: those who are at ease, Psalms
s: scoff_at the speakers (we/our) Those who are at ease are described as the source of scoffing that exceedingly fills the speakers' soul. They are named alongside the proud, whose contempt is also mentioned.

The speakers say they have endured much contempt, which is the reason they ask the LORD for mercy. It is also described as coming from the proud, and it fills their soul together with the scoffing of those at ease.
